passage:
The nearest de-addiction centre was in Siliguri, two hours by bus, and Binita had exactly ₹600 left in her account. She had rehearsed the words all night.
In the morning she found her brother Divyansh feeding the hens behind their house in Kurseong and said it before she could lose her nerve. "Dada, I've been drinking every day since the tea garden job ended. I can't stop by myself. I need help."
He set the bowl down slowly. She braced for shouting.
Instead he said, "Okay. Thank you for telling me. What do we do first?"
Together they looked up the government hospital's de-addiction clinic. The consultation there was free. Divyansh said he would pay the bus fare and go with her on Thursday. "And don't worry about Ma," he said. "We'll tell her together, after the doctor."
Binita's legs shook all the way back inside, but they held.

qa.q: How far away was the nearest de-addiction centre?
qa.a: It was in Siliguri, two hours by bus.

qa.q: Why did Binita brace for shouting?
qa.a: She expected anger and shame from her brother, and the fear of his reaction had been building all night.

qa.q: What steps did Binita and Divyansh take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: She told someone safe, and together they found a free government de-addiction clinic, with Divyansh paying the fare and going along, so she wouldn't face recovery alone.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt hearing Binita's words by the hens?
qa.a: He may have been shocked and worried, yet he chose to thank her and ask what to do first, putting support ahead of blame.

grounding: Shows a young woman telling her brother about her drinking and, despite little money and distance, contacting a de-addiction clinic with family support.

passage:
Ojas had typed the message four times before sending it: "Trisha, can you come over? I need to tell you something and I'm scared."
His cousin reached the Indiranagar flat in twenty minutes, still wearing her office lanyard. He showed her everything: the betting apps, the three loans, the ₹2.8 lakh he owed. His voice cracked twice.
Trisha read it all without a word, then took a long breath. "Okay. I'm not going anywhere. Who do we call first?"
They found a hospital de-addiction service that treated gambling problems and booked the earliest appointment, Tuesday. Trisha also found a support group that met on Friday evenings in Domlur.
"And your parents?" she asked.
Ojas's face crumpled. "They'll think I'm a disgrace."
"Your mother is tougher than you think," Trisha said. "We'll tell them together, with the doctor's name in hand."

qa.q: How much did Ojas owe?
qa.a: ₹2.8 lakh.

qa.q: What is Ojas afraid his parents will think?
qa.a: He fears they will think he is a disgrace, which shows how much shame he still carries.

qa.q: What made Ojas's first steps towards help solid?
qa.a: He told someone safe, and with Trisha he booked a de-addiction appointment, found a support group and planned to tell his parents together.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel as she reads through the apps and loans?
qa.a: Trisha is probably shocked and worried, but chooses calm support, saying 'I'm not going anywhere' and moving straight to next steps.

grounding: Illustrates a young man telling a safe person about gambling debts and, with her help, contacting a de-addiction service and support group.

passage:
"Kalyani didi, can I come in?"
"Jatin? It's midnight. What's wrong?"
"I need to tell you something. I've been using. Pills. For a year. I can't stop."
Kalyani sat down slowly. "Okay. Thank you for telling me."
"You're not angry?"
"I'm scared. But I'm not ashamed of you. Have you told anyone else?"
"No. I looked up a de-addiction centre. I just couldn't call."
"Then we call together. In the morning. I'll sit with you."
"What if they judge me?"
"Then we find someone else. You're not doing this alone."
Jatin let out a long breath.

qa.q: What does Jatin say he has been using?
qa.a: Pills.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he asked "You're not angry?"
qa.a: Jatin felt afraid and ashamed, expecting to be judged for the confession.

qa.q: Why is Kalyani's response helpful at this stage?
qa.a: Kalyani gives thanks for the honesty, says there is no shame, and offers to call the de-addiction centre together in the morning.

qa.q: What is Kalyani experiencing as she listens?
qa.a: Kalyani says she is scared, and seems shaken but steady and loving.

grounding: Shows a young person telling a sister about an addiction and planning to contact a de-addiction centre together, supported without shame.

passage:
Looking back, the hardest call I ever made was to my husband, Bhupen, from the car park at work. I said, "I need to tell you something. I've been drinking every day. I've been hiding it. I need help."
He was quiet. Then he said, "I'm coming. Don't drive."
That evening we sat with our family doctor. She didn't lecture. She referred me to a counsellor and a support group that meets on Tuesdays. Bhupen came to the first meeting and held my hand.
My mother-in-law said, "We're not ashamed of you, Indu beti. We're proud you asked." I've never forgotten that.
Recovery wasn't something I did alone. It was something we did.

qa.q: When does the support group meet?
qa.a: On Tuesdays.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when she made the call from the car park?
qa.a: She felt scared and ashamed, but determined to stop hiding and ask for help.

qa.q: What made Indu's steps towards recovery work?
qa.a: Telling someone safe, seeing the doctor, joining a counsellor and support group, and having a family that offered support without shame.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt on the phone?
qa.a: Bhupen was probably shocked and worried, but chose to come immediately and support her.

grounding: Shows a young woman telling her husband about her drinking and contacting a doctor, counsellor and support group, with family support.

passage:
De-addiction clinic intake note, Monday
Jagdish, 24, arrived with his father this morning. He said, "I've been using for two years. I told my father last night. I want to stop." His hands were shaking. His father sat beside him, holding his arm, and said once, quietly, "We're with you."
Jagdish said the hardest part was telling someone. He had rehearsed it for weeks. When I asked what helped him finally speak, he said, "My father didn't shout."
We have started an assessment, and he will join the outpatient group on Wednesdays. I have also given his father the details of our family support group.
Hafsa, clinic counsellor

qa.q: When will Jagdish join the outpatient group?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he arrived at the clinic?
qa.a: He felt nervous and afraid, his hands shaking, but determined to stop.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's plan include, and why does it help?
qa.a: An assessment, the Wednesday outpatient group, and a family support group for his father, because recovery works better with support.

qa.q: What might Jagdish's father be experiencing at the clinic?
qa.a: His father is probably frightened and sad, but chooses steady support, saying "We're with you."

grounding: Shows a counsellor's note on a young man who told his father and came to a clinic for help, supported without shame.

passage:
Monday night.
I did it. At 9 a.m., before I could talk myself out of it, I called the de-addiction helpline the doctor at the clinic gave me last month. A counsellor called back at noon and booked me for Thursday. She asked the questions I'd been dodging for two years, and I answered them.
Then the harder part. I told Bhavna didi. I'd planned a whole speech and forgot it. I just said, "Didi, I drink every night and I can't stop by myself." She put down her phone, came and sat next to me, and said, "Vishal, thank you for telling me. We'll go on Thursday together." No lecture. No "how could you". She cried a little, then made us both rice.
I feel scared and lighter at the same time. The counsellor said recovery isn't a one-person job. Tonight, for the first time, it doesn't feel like one.

qa.q: When is Vishal's appointment?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel after telling Bhavna didi?
qa.a: Vishal feels scared and lighter at the same time, and less alone.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's reply do right?
qa.a: She thanked Vishal, offered to go on Thursday together and gave no lecture: support without shame.

qa.q: What might Bhavna be feeling when she cries a little?
qa.a: She may be sad and shaken by the news but also relieved to be told, and she chooses to stay steady for Vishal.

grounding: Shows a person telling a safe family member and contacting a counsellor through a helpline, and the family offering support without shame.
